summary: Describes how Change-of-Authorization and Disconnect messages from RFC 5176 can be proxied in RADIUS when networks use realm-based proxying as defined in RFC 7542. It updates RFC 5176 and also updates RFC 5580 to allow the Operator-Name attribute in CoA-Request packets. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a network needs to tell a user's connection to change or stop, and the message must pass through several middle servers. This document explains how to pass such messages along correctly.

subtitle: How RADIUS Change-of-Authorization and Disconnect messages can travel back through proxies from a home network to the visited network.

tldr.problem: RFC 5176 says Change-of-Authorization and Disconnect messages can be proxied but gives no way to do it, so in practice proxying them is impossible when a user roams between networks.
tldr.mechanism: Visited networks put an Operator-Name attribute, plus a new opaque Operator-NAS-Identifier attribute, into the Access-Request and Accounting-Request packets they send out. The home network returns them in CoA packets, and proxies route on the realm in Operator-Name.
tldr.outcome: Realm-based CoA proxying works without proxies tracking user sessions. It updates RFC 5176 and RFC 5580, and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8559 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 5176 and RFC 5580, and does not change the status of RFC 5176.

sections.title: The Problem with Proxying CoA
sections.content:
RFC 5176 defines Change-of-Authorization (CoA) and Disconnect Message behavior for RADIUS, and says proxying these messages is possible, but it does not say how. The result is that in practice proxying CoA packets is impossible.

The RFC explains why. Proxies are normally stateless with respect to user sessions, and in a roaming consortium a proxy may forward traffic for tens of millions of users, so tracking sessions does not scale. Even a proxy that did track sessions could not match a CoA packet to a session, because RFC 5176 does not say which attributes identify a session. The CoA server may also not be co-located with the RADIUS client, and tying the reverse path to the forward path would block failover to another CoA server.

The fix is to route the reverse path by realm, just as the forward path is, but using an attribute other than User-Name. This applies only to realm-based proxying as defined in RFC 7542. It does not change any other RADIUS system. The document is on the Standards Track because it updates RFC 5580, which is itself a Standards Track document.
sections.eli5: A letter has to travel back through several post offices, but nobody wrote down which road it took. This document adds a return-address label that every post office can read.

sections.title: Routing Backwards with Operator-Name
sections.content:
Normal proxying uses the realm in the user's Network Access Identifier (NAI) in User-Name to pick the next hop. For CoA going back to the visited network, that would send the packet to the home network, where the session is not. So proxies MUST NOT use the NAI in User-Name to route CoA packets.

Instead they use the Operator-Name attribute from RFC 5580. For the REALM namespace it holds an ASCII 1 followed by the visited network's realm, such as 1example.com. A visited network that wants CoA proxying SHOULD put it into Access-Request and Accounting-Request packets it proxies outward, and MUST use one consistent value for any one user session. Home networks that expect to send CoA MUST record it per session.

When the home network sends a CoA-Request or Disconnect-Request it MUST include the recorded Operator-Name. The logical realm routing table from RFC 7542 is extended with a mapping from realm to next-hop CoA servers, and lookups for CoA use the CoA server field. If the realm is unknown, the proxy MUST return a NAK with Error-Cause 502 (Request Not Routable). The RFC also updates RFC 5580 so that CoA-Request and Disconnect-Request may carry zero or one Operator-Name.
sections.eli5: The visited network stamps its own name on the outgoing mail. When the home network wants to reply, it copies that stamp, and every post office along the way reads it to know which direction to go.

sections.title: The Operator-NAS-Identifier Attribute
sections.content:
Reaching the visited network is not enough: it must find the right Network Access Server (NAS). NAS-Identifier, NAS-IP-Address and NAS-IPv6-Address are unreliable because proxies often rewrite them or they may be removed to keep the visited network's internals private. So the RFC defines the new Operator-NAS-Identifier attribute, an opaque token only the visited network can interpret.

It has type 241.8, allocated from the short extended space, data type string, and length 4 to 35. Implementations MUST handle 1 to 32 octets of data and MUST NOT create more than 64. It MAY appear in Access-Request, Accounting-Request, CoA-Request and Disconnect-Request packets, only alongside an Operator-Name, and at most once per packet.

The visited network SHOULD add it to outgoing requests. When it does, it SHOULD delete NAS-IP-Address, NAS-IPv6-Address and NAS-Identifier, and then MUST add a new NAS-Identifier containing the visited network's realm name. No other proxy or server may add it.

The value can be built two ways: keep a database that maps each NAS to a token, or obfuscate the NAS IP address with locally known information, for example by XORing it with a secret key. No integrity check is required, because tampering would only get the request rejected.
sections.eli5: Inside the visited network there are lots of doors. The label is a coat-check ticket that only that network can read, so the message finds the right door without outsiders seeing the building's plan.

sections.title: Requirements on Each Party
sections.content:
A home server MUST store Operator-NAS-Identifier along with its other session identification attributes and include it verbatim in any CoA packet for that session. It MUST NOT send CoA packets for users of other networks.

A visited network MUST apply the proxy rules, use the Operator-NAS-Identifier to choose the NAS, and MUST remove Operator-Name and Operator-NAS-Identifier before the packet goes to the NAS. It MUST also ensure that the packet carries one of NAS-IP-Address, NAS-IPv6-Address or NAS-Identifier. It validates the realm in Operator-Name and, if it is not one of its own, MUST return a NAK with Error-Cause 502. It SHOULD also check that the home network is allowed to send it CoA, and if the NAS is unknown MUST return Error-Cause 403 (NAS Identification Mismatch).

Proxies MUST perform a reverse path forwarding check that a CoA packet comes from an authorized Dynamic Authorization Client, strengthening the RFC 5176 text from MAY to MUST, and return 502 if it fails. Proxies SHOULD forward packets as is or with minimal changes, MUST NOT treat all attributes as mandatory, MUST pass Operator-Name and Operator-NAS-Identifier through unchanged, and MUST undo on the reverse path any attribute edits made on the forward path. The NAS, for its part, MUST NOT treat as mandatory attributes that cannot affect the session, such as Proxy-State.
sections.eli5: Each helper has a short job list. The home server must keep the labels safe, the middle servers must pass them along untouched, and the visited network must peel them off before handing the message to the right device.

sections.title: How a Session Flows End to End
sections.content:
At login, a roaming user connects through a NAS in the visited network. The NAS sends an Access-Request to the visited RADIUS server, which adds Operator-Name (for example 1example.com), may add Operator-NAS-Identifier, and edits the NAS identification attributes as described above. It proxies the request upstream until it reaches the home server, which records the attributes with the rest of the session information.

Later the home server decides to change the session's authorization or disconnect the user. It looks up the recorded attributes, finds the next-hop CoA server for that realm in its routing table and sends the CoA-Request. Each proxy repeats the lookup until the packet reaches the visited network.

The visited network uses Operator-NAS-Identifier to find the NAS (or, if absent, another method such as a local session database), removes the two attributes, adds back a NAS identification attribute and sends the packet on. The response returns to the home network the normal way. If a proxy finds no destination or no Operator-Name, it replies with CoA-NAK and Error-Cause 502. If the visited network finds no CoA server it replies with Error-Cause 403.
sections.eli5: The message goes out stamped with where it came from. When it needs to go back, it follows the stamps home in reverse, and at the last stop the stamps are removed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC incorporates the security discussion in Section 11 of RFC 6929 and says RADIUS proxying has many inherent security issues. Packets are signed hop by hop with a shared secret, so any intermediate proxy can forge, replay or modify packets, and the security of the whole chain rests largely on trust rather than technical means. There is no end-to-end security between visited and home networks.

The RFC argues that CoA proxying adds little. The proxies that see CoA packets are the same ones that already see Access-Request and Accounting-Request packets, and a proxy can already change authorization in an Access-Accept. The main new capability is that home networks can disconnect or change users in a visited network, which requires mutual agreement and only applies to parties who can already control user sessions.

Nothing depends on the secrecy of Operator-NAS-Identifier. The process would work if it simply held the NAS IP address; an opaque token is used only because there is no reason to expose that information. IANA allocated 241.8 for it from the short extended space of the RADIUS Attribute Types registry.
sections.eli5: Every middle server could in theory fake a message, so this still depends on trusting the servers in the chain. The new labels do not make that any worse.
